column5: UK CMO foreword (2026 update): benefits are largest going from none to some activity and build rapidly to around 150 minutes a week, then rise more slowly; if you do none, do some, and if you do some, do a bit more. Benefits far outweigh risks even for most people with long-term conditions, and the least active gain most. Lasting change is most likely when activity is enjoyable, useful or part of routine.

UK CMO foreword (2026): people who have recently been inactive (for example after an operation) or who are taking GLP-1 agonist drugs especially need activities that maintain muscle strength. A current, UK-specific special-population point for the coaching of clients on weight-loss medication; stay in scope (no medication advice).

UK CMO adult guideline (19 to 64, updated 10/07/2026): be active every day; each week accumulate at least 150 minutes of moderate activity, or 75 minutes of vigorous activity, or even shorter durations of very vigorous activity (sprinting, stair climbing), or a combination; strength activities for the major muscle groups on at least 2 days a week, any strengthening better than none; minimise sedentary time and break up long periods with at least light activity. The course teaches the WHO 150 to 300 range and tells UK learners to check the CMO wording: it can now teach the UK wording directly, which sets a minimum ('at least 150') rather than a range and adds a very vigorous option.

UK CMO executive summary: benefits rise steadily but substantially up to the recommended amount and more slowly beyond it; the guidelines are not absolute thresholds, with benefits recognised both above and below 150 minutes a week. Prolonged sitting is harmful even in people who meet the activity guidelines, though the evidence does not support a specific sitting time limit. Matches and sharpens the course's 'some is better than none' and no-threshold sedentary teaching.

UK CMO: strengthening activities in adults and older adults help maintain strength and delay the natural decline in muscle mass and bone density which occurs from around 50 years of age. Older adults (65+): activities for muscle strength, balance and flexibility on at least 2 days a week; 150 minutes moderate aerobic built up gradually (or 75 vigorous if already active); weight-bearing activity for bone; break up sitting with light activity or at least standing.

UK CMO introduction: intensity is relative to the person; the talk test separates them (able to talk but not sing = moderate; difficulty talking without pausing = vigorous). Greater intensity brings more benefit for the same time, but light activity at higher volumes may give the same benefits and is a more achievable route in. Gains are especially large for people doing fewer than 30 minutes a week. No minimum amount is needed for some benefit; a 10-minute target can be a useful behavioural goal for beginners, and bouts under 10 minutes also count.

UK CMO on risk: the risk of serious adverse events from physical activity is very low and benefits outweigh risks, including for disabled adults at an appropriate dose. Musculoskeletal injury is more common in impact activities; adverse cardiac events are rare and inversely associated with the volume of regularly performed vigorous activity; greater intensity carries greater injury risk, especially in people unaccustomed to exercise. Starting at low durations and intensities and building up is the safest way to progress. A UK primary source for the screening module's 'why we screen' lesson.

UK CMO on weight: diet is the important factor in weight management; activity plays a supporting role, reduces cardiovascular risk in people with overweight or obesity irrespective of weight change, and helps prevent regain. On GLP-1 agonist drugs both fat and muscle decrease; they are licensed only alongside physical activity and behaviour change, and muscle-strengthening activity is likely to matter particularly for keeping muscle and preventing regain (evidence still emerging).

UK CMO: strength work should cover all the major muscle groups; bone strengthening needs moderate and high impact activity; balance training reduces falls; different activities affect muscle, bone and balance differently, so include a variety. Supports session design across movement patterns.

UK CMO adults (2026 evidence update): regular strength work should be considered as important as reaching 150 minutes of aerobic activity; evidence supports muscle strengthening of all main muscle groups 1 to 2 times a week, with measurable benefit from over 30 and up to 120 minutes a week, but not enough evidence to set a duration. Strength benefits on mortality are strongest combined with aerobic activity. The 150 minutes can come in bouts of any length and even in one or 2 sessions a week.

UK CMO sedentary evidence: meta-analysis of 34 studies and over a million people links more than 6 to 8 hours a day of total sitting and 3 to 4 hours of TV with greater all-cause and cardiovascular mortality; a recent review estimated about 5% higher cardiovascular-event risk per extra daily hour of sitting; activity reduces the association. Still no official sitting limit. Adds concrete numbers to the course's sedentary lesson.

UK CMO: any vigorous activity is associated with lower risk of premature death, with further reduction at higher vigorous volumes; for hypertension, 150 minutes a week cuts risk by about 6% with further reductions for each extra 150 minutes. Light activity done for longer can match moderate activity's benefits.

UK CMO pregnancy and postpartum: activity can safely be recommended during and after pregnancy with no negative effect on breastfeeding; choices should reflect pre-pregnancy activity and include strength training; vigorous activity is not recommended for previously inactive women; after the 6 to 8 week postnatal check, intensity can build from moderate to vigorous over at least 3 months. Benefits include fewer hypertensive disorders, lower gestational diabetes risk, less postpartum depression.

UK CMO: more than 150 minutes of activity plus dietary restriction may be needed for weight loss, and how much extra activity produces loss cannot be specified; activity helps maintain weight after loss. A 2018 review found no evidence that appropriate activity is a risk for disabled adults; myths that activity is inherently harmful for disabled people should be dispelled.

UK CMO older adults: loss of muscle strength is the primary limiting factor for independence; evidence-based strength and balance programmes reduce falls. Three groups: active older adults (twice weekly resistance, some impact such as skipping, balance such as standing on one leg or walking backwards); 'in transition' (walk and rest for a minute, sit-to-stands, stair climbing, home strength and balance); frail (more light activity, less sitting, sit-to-stands, short walks, longer duration rather than intensity). For frailty, moderate-to-severe dementia, previous vertebral fractures or regular falls, new exercises may best be supervised by a trained professional at first.

UK CMO older adults evidence: 30 minutes a day of moderate to vigorous activity on top of daily life equals roughly 7,000 to 10,000 steps a day; 4,500 to 5,500 steps a day for health-related quality of life. Regular moderate activity almost halves the risk of disability progressing; there is very limited evidence on high-intensity interval training in older people. The old 10-minute minimum bout was removed.
UK CMO conclusion: the next update of the UK guidelines is anticipated jointly with the WHO, published in 2030. Note for the course's stale-source schedule.
